981.title: Krishna pays his guru
981.hook: with Kamsa gone, Krishna goes to school, and the teacher's fee is a boy the ocean took
981.carry: the teacher is honored like a god
981.tomorrow: does Krishna remember the people who raised him?
981.howItsDone: Hindus honor teachers by touching their feet and on Guru Purnima, and the custom of guru dakshina, a gift to a teacher at the end of study, continues in some traditional music, dance and scriptural schools; Krishna's fee to Sandipani is one story told when people speak of what a student owes a teacher.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Gita Govinda with a practice of bhakti, smarana: bring the beloved back to mind, again and again.
screen: `BHAKTI.` · `SMARANA: REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: Kamsa is dead. His father Ugrasena is back on the throne of Mathura. Vasudeva and Devaki have their sons again. So what does the hero of the story do next? He goes to school. The Bhagavata's tenth book picks up the thread right after the arena, and sends Krishna and his brother Balarama to study with a teacher in the city of Avanti, a brahmin named Sandipani. They sit at his feet like any other students. And when it's time to pay, the teacher asks for something no student could give.
screen: `KAMSA IS GONE.` → `THE HERO GOES TO SCHOOL.` → `A FEE NO STUDENT COULD PAY.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata, Krishna is the Lord himself. Why would he need a teacher? The text's answer, in paraphrase: the brothers, though they were the source of all knowledge, chose to live in a teacher's house to show the world how it's done. They serve Sandipani and learn fast. Then comes the fee, the guru dakshina, the gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end. Sandipani and his wife ask for the one thing they can't stop grieving: their son, lost in the ocean at Prabhasa. Not gold. Their boy. At the shore, the ocean tells the brothers that a demon living in the shape of a conch, Panchajana, took the child. Krishna goes into the water, overcomes him, and takes the conch shell. The boy isn't there. So Krishna goes all the way to the city of Yama, the lord of death, and blows that conch at the gate. Yama comes out, honors him, and gives the child back, and the brothers hand their teacher his son. Here's the teaching under it. Hindus honor the guru, the teacher, like a god. An old Upanishad sends students home with that line: let your mother be a god to you, and your father, and your teacher. It's why students touch a teacher's feet, why there's a day for teachers, Guru Purnima, and why the gift at the end isn't a fee that settles the account. If the Lord himself sits at a teacher's feet, and goes to the gate of death to thank him, the rest of us can bow. That conch, Panchajanya, stays in the story: at the start of the Gita, it's the conch Krishna blows.
screen: `WHY WOULD THE LORD NEED A TEACHER?` · `THE FEE: OUR LOST SON.` · `A CONCH AT YAMA'S GATE.` · `THE TEACHER, HONORED LIKE A GOD.` · then, large: `GURU DAKSHINA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one teacher who changed something for you: a schoolteacher, a grandparent, a coach, someone at work. Picture one thing they said, then ask quietly what you would give them, if you could, and let the answer come. If you pray, hold that teacher in your prayer; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with thanks.
Guru dakshina. The gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end. Today, Krishna as a student, and a teacher's fee paid at the gate of death.
screen: `GURU DAKSHINA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the teacher is honored like a god. Krishna paid his at the gate of death. Day nine hundred eighty-one, done.

982.title: Uddhava in Vraja
982.hook: a learned friend arrives in Vraja at sunset, and a father asks him one question all night
982.carry: loving God like your own child
982.tomorrow: why would Krishna run from a fight?
982.howItsDone: In Vaishnava traditions, the chapters of Uddhava's visit to Vraja are read aloud in Bhagavata recitations and sung in devotional songs, Nanda and Yashoda are honored as models of vatsalya, parental love for Krishna, and many families keep a small image of baby Krishna, often called Bal Gopal or Laddu Gopal, bathed, dressed and fed each morning.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: guru dakshina, Krishna as a student, and a teacher honored like a god.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `GURU DAKSHINA.`

segments.voice: In Mathura, Krishna calls his friend and counselor Uddhava aside. Go to Vraja, he tells him. Comfort my father and mother. Comfort the gopis. Tell them what I've told you. So Uddhava drives out to the village Krishna grew up in, and arrives at sunset. The cows are coming home, raising dust. Calves are calling. There's the sound of milking, lamps being lit, butter being churned. An ordinary evening in a place that has been missing someone for a long time. The first to meet him is Nanda, Krishna's foster father.
screen: `GO TO VRAJA. COMFORT THEM.` → `SUNSET. COWS COMING HOME.` → `NANDA MEETS HIM AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Nanda embraces Uddhava as if he were Krishna himself, washes his feet, feeds him, and sits him down. Then the questions, in paraphrase. Is he well? Does Krishna remember us? Will he come back, even once, so we can see his face? Nanda starts remembering out loud: the forest fire, the serpent in the river, the storm. He can't finish. His voice breaks. Beside him, Yashoda listens to every word, and the text says her tears won't stop. Uddhava answers as a learned man would. You two are truly fortunate, he says, to love him like this. Then he says something large. Krishna isn't only your son. He has no mother or father of his own, no one who is his and no one who isn't. He is within everyone, the Self of all beings. Will that help a mother whose tears won't stop? The Bhagavata doesn't pretend it does. It lets them talk through the whole night. Vaishnava teachers have a name for Nanda and Yashoda's love: vatsalya, loving God the way a parent loves a child. The big truth, he's in everyone, sits right beside the small grief, does he remember us, and the learned man calls the grieving parents fortunate. Then morning comes. The women of Vraja are up churning butter, singing about Krishna as they churn, and the song carries over the village. It's why many Hindu homes keep a small baby Krishna who is bathed, dressed and fed each morning: God, loved as your own child.
screen: `DOES HE REMEMBER US?` · `NANDA REMEMBERS, AND BREAKS.` · `HE IS THE SELF OF ALL.` · `VATSALYA: LOVING GOD AS YOUR CHILD.` · then, large: `AT DAWN, THEY CHURN AND SING.`

segments.voice: Let the body be heavy on the chair and picture Krishna as Yashoda knew him: a small child, butter on his hands. If you pray, offer him something small in your mind, a little butter or a sweet, the way many families do each morning, with a parent's tenderness. If you don't, bring to mind a household that is missing someone and just sit in that house for a minute, the way Uddhava sat with Nanda, listening.
Uddhava, Krishna's trusted friend and counselor, sent to comfort the family he left behind. Today, a father who asks if he's remembered, and a love Vaishnavas call vatsalya.
screen: `UDDHAVA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: loving God like your own child. Vatsalya, Yashoda's love, which the learned Uddhava called fortunate. See you tomorrow.

983.title: Muchukunda asks for nothing
983.hook: an army at the gate, Krishna runs into a cave, and an old king inside is offered anything
983.tomorrow: what does a princess do when she's promised to the wrong man?
983.howItsDone: In parts of Gujarat, Krishna is worshipped as Ranchhod or Ranchhodrai, the one who left the battlefield, and devotees tell the story of the chase to Muchukunda's cave as part of that name's meaning; Muchukunda's prayer for nothing but Krishna is told in Bhagavata recitations as a picture of devotion that wants nothing back.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddhava with Nanda, and Yashoda's love for God as her own child.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `DOES HE REMEMBER US?`

segments.voice: Mathura has no peace. Jarasandha, the powerful king whose daughters were married to Kamsa, attacks the city again and again. Krishna turns his armies back each time, and each time Jarasandha returns. Now a second enemy marches on the city too, a fierce king called Kalayavana, with a vast army. Two forces, one city. And the Bhagavata gives its hero a strange move. Krishna walks out through the city gate, alone, without a weapon, wearing a garland, and lets the enemy king see him. Then he turns and runs.
screen: `JARASANDHA, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `KALAYAVANA AT THE GATE.` → `KRISHNA WALKS OUT, AND RUNS.`

segments.voice: First, he protects his people. Before he steps outside, Krishna has a new city built in the sea, Dwaraka, and the text says he moves the people of Mathura there by his own power, so they wake up somewhere safe. Only then does he walk out. Kalayavana recognizes him from what he's heard and, being proud, chases him on foot, man to man. Krishna stays just out of reach, up into the hills and into a mountain cave. Kalayavana charges in and sees a man lying asleep. Thinking it's Krishna, he kicks him. The sleeper is Muchukunda, an ancient king who once fought for the gods and asked them, as his reward, for sleep. He wakes, looks at the man who kicked him, and the text says that at his glance Kalayavana burns to ashes. Then Krishna shows himself, and here is the heart of the chapter. Krishna offers the old king any boon he likes. Muchukunda says no. In paraphrase: I spent my life chasing kingdoms and pride, and it was a trap; now I want nothing but shelter at your feet. And Krishna is pleased that the offer didn't tempt him. That's the Bhagavata's picture of the highest devotion: loving God for God, not for what God can give. Hindus pray for things all the time, health, a child, an exam, and the Gita calls those who come asking noble too. But the devotee these stories hold up is the one who asks for God himself. And the runaway? Gujarat still loves Krishna as Ranchhod, explained by devotees as the one who left the battlefield. There, it's a title of love.
screen: `FIRST, A CITY IN THE SEA.` · `THE CHASE INTO THE CAVE.` · `THE SLEEPER WAKES: MUCHUKUNDA.` · `ANY BOON? ONLY YOU.` · then, large: `ASK GOD FOR GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind what you usually ask for: health, a grade, a fix at home. Asking is allowed; let those wishes sit to one side for a minute. Then, like Muchukunda, ask for nothing at all. If you pray, simply say a name you love, wanting only to be near; if you don't, sit with what you love most without wanting anything from it.
Ranchhod, the one who left the battlefield, a loving name for Krishna in Gujarat. Today, the chase into Muchukunda's cave, and a king who asked for nothing but Krishna.
screen: `RANCHHOD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: asking God for God himself. Muchukunda was offered anything, and asked for that. That's day nine hundred eighty-three.

984.title: Rukmini's letter
984.hook: a princess is about to be married to the wrong man, so she writes a letter and finds someone to carry it
984.tomorrow: who stole the jewel that shone like the sun?
984.howItsDone: Rukmini is worshipped beside Krishna in temples, and some Hindus recite her letter from the Bhagavata, especially when praying for a good marriage; at a Bhagavata saptaha, seven days of the book read aloud, simply listening is the devotion.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ranchhod, and Muchukunda, who was offered anything and asked for Krishna himself.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `RANCHHOD.`

segments.voice: A letter is traveling by road from the kingdom of Vidarbha to the city of Dwaraka. The man carrying it is an old brahmin, trusted, sworn to deliver it into one pair of hands. The woman who wrote it is the king's daughter, Rukmini. Her brother has arranged her marriage to a king she doesn't want: Shishupala, the man we met earlier this year at Yudhishthira's great rite. The wedding is coming. Her family has decided. And Rukmini has decided too, quietly, on her own.
screen: `A LETTER ON THE ROAD TO DWARAKA.` → `A WEDDING SHE DIDN'T CHOOSE.` → `RUKMINI HAS DECIDED.`

segments.voice: In Dwaraka, Krishna receives the brahmin, washes his feet, feeds him, and only then asks why he's come. The brahmin hands him the letter, and the Bhagavata lets us read it, in paraphrase. I have heard of your qualities, Rukmini writes, and hearing them, my mind has gone to you and won't come back. I've set shame aside. I have chosen you. Come and take my hand. Don't let the king of Chedi take what is yours, like a jackal stealing a lion's share. Then she gives him a plan. Come to Vidarbha before the wedding, unseen, with your forces. She knows her family's customs: before the wedding, the bride walks out of the city to the temple of the goddess Ambika. That's where you'll find me. And if you don't come, she writes, she will give up her life, and keep hoping for him life after life. Rukmini has never seen Krishna. She has only heard about him. That's a teaching, not a detail: Prahlada's list of the nine ways of devotion begins with shravana, hearing, and it's why Hindus still gather for days just to listen to the Bhagavata read aloud. But she doesn't stop at hearing. She writes, she plans, she risks. Krishna answers right away, setting out in his chariot that same night. On the appointed day, Rukmini prays at the goddess's temple, walks out, and he's there. He lifts her into his chariot in front of everyone. There's a fight; her brother chases them, and loses. In Dwaraka, they marry. Some devotees hear Rukmini as the soul that has heard of God, chosen God, and taken the first step.
screen: `I HAVE HEARD, AND I HAVE CHOSEN.` · `A PLAN: THE GODDESS'S TEMPLE.` · `SHRAVANA: SHE NEVER SAW HIM. SHE HEARD.` · `HE COMES THAT SAME NIGHT.` · then, large: `COME AND TAKE MY HAND.`

segments.voice: Rukmini's devotion started with hearing, so for this sit, simply listen: the far sounds, the near ones, the sound of your own breath, received one by one without naming or judging them. If you pray, let a name you love be the sound you return to; if you don't, return to the breath whenever the mind wanders.
Rukmini, the princess of Vidarbha who became Krishna's queen. Today, her letter: devotion that begins with shravana, hearing, and then writes, plans and acts.

985.title: Jambavan knows his Lord
985.hook: a jewel goes missing, a rumor blames Krishna, and a bear in a cave knows him from long ago
985.carry: one Lord, come again as Rama and Krishna
985.tomorrow: what can a poor man bring the richest friend he has?
985.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes and temples keep Rama and Krishna side by side as forms of Vishnu; the Syamantaka story is told in Bhagavata recitations, and in some regions it is read or heard on Ganesh Chaturthi, as a story about false accusation and how it is cleared.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rukmini's letter, and shravana, devotion that begins by hearing, then chooses.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `I HAVE HEARD. I HAVE CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: Someone is walking toward Dwaraka so bright that people in the streets shield their eyes. They run to Krishna: the sun god himself is coming to see you! Krishna laughs. It isn't the sun, he tells them. It's Satrajit, wearing his jewel. The jewel is the Syamantaka, a gift to Satrajit from the sun. It's beautiful, and it brings wealth to whoever keeps it. Before long, it will go missing. And the city will start whispering a name. Krishna's.

segments.voice: Here's how it goes wrong, in paraphrase. Krishna asks Satrajit to give the jewel to the king, Ugrasena. Satrajit refuses. Not long after, his brother Prasena wears it out hunting and doesn't come back. A lion kills him and takes the jewel; then a bear kills the lion and carries it to his cave. The people of Dwaraka only know that Krishna asked for the jewel, and now it's gone. So people talk. Krishna doesn't argue; he goes and finds out. He follows the trail to a dark cave and goes in alone. The bear is Jambavan, the bear king who served Rama in the Ramayana, ages before. They fight in the dark, on and on, until Jambavan realizes that no one but his own Lord could be this strong. It's Rama, come again in a new form. He bows, gives up the jewel, and gives his daughter Jambavati in marriage too. Back in Dwaraka, Krishna returns the jewel before everyone, and Satrajit, ashamed, gives him his daughter Satyabhama. Now the teaching inside that cave. Hindus call it avatara: God coming down into the world. In the Gita, Krishna says that whenever dharma falls and wrong rises, he comes, age after age, to protect the good. So Rama and Krishna aren't rivals, or two gods to choose between. For Vaishnavas they're one Lord, Vishnu, come again. An old servant of Rama knew him in the dark. It's why many homes keep Rama and Krishna on the same shelf.
screen: `THE JEWEL GOES MISSING.` · `HE DOESN'T ARGUE. HE FINDS OUT.` · `JAMBAVAN KNOWS HIS LORD.` · `AVATARA: GOD COMES AGAIN.` · then, large: `RAMA AND KRISHNA: ONE LORD.`

If you pray, say it slowly a few times, or simply say the two names, Rama, Krishna, as one prayer; if you don't, rest with the thought that what is good can come back into the world again and again.

986.title: Sudama's flattened rice
986.hook: a poor man visits his richest friend, forgets to ask for anything, and walks home happy anyway
986.carry: God receives the love, not the size
986.tomorrow: why does the kirtan's first song go to Ganesha?
986.howItsDone: Hindus tell the story of Sudama, also called Kuchela in South India, as a picture of friendship with God, and in some places devotees offer flattened rice to Krishna in memory of it.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Syamantaka jewel, and Jambavan, who knew Krishna as his Lord Rama, come again.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `HE GIVES THE JEWEL BACK.`

segments.voice: A thin man in a torn cloth stands at the gates of Dwaraka, holding a small bundle. He's a brahmin, poor enough that his family often goes hungry. His wife sent him: go to your old friend, the one you studied with as a boy. He's the lord of Dwaraka now. Surely he'll help. The man didn't want to ask. He came mostly to see his friend's face. In the bundle is the only gift his house could find: a few handfuls of flattened rice, begged from the neighbors. Tradition calls him Sudama.
screen: `A POOR MAN AT THE GATES.` → `GO TO YOUR OLD FRIEND.` → `A BUNDLE OF FLATTENED RICE.`

segments.voice: Krishna sees him from across the palace, leaves his seat beside Rukmini, runs to him, and embraces him. He washes his friend's feet. They talk about their school days at Sandipani's house, and the night a storm caught them gathering firewood, holding hands in the dark until their teacher found them at dawn and blessed them. Then Krishna asks, smiling: what did you bring me? The brahmin is too ashamed to show it. So Krishna takes the bundle himself and eats a handful of the rice with delight. As he reaches for more, Rukmini gently catches his hand, as if to say: that's enough. That one handful is plenty for everything your friend will ever need. In the morning he walks home. He never asked. Krishna never offered. And he goes happy, thinking, in paraphrase: he didn't give me wealth, so that I wouldn't become proud and forget him. He reaches his village and can't find his hut. In its place is a house shining like a palace, and his wife comes out to meet him. The Bhagavata gives him a last reflection: Krishna gives a great deal and counts it as little, and takes a small thing from his devotee and counts it as a great deal. In the Gita, Krishna says it outright: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love, I accept. That's why Hindus offer God food, flowers and water every day, and share it back as prasad. What God receives is the love, not the size. The brahmin lives on in that house, his heart where it was. On Krishna.
screen: `KRISHNA RUNS TO HIM.` · `ONE HANDFUL IS ENOUGH.` · `HE NEVER ASKED.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, WITH LOVE.` · then, large: `GOD RECEIVES THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Take one small thing near you: a glass of water, a piece of fruit, a flower from outside. Hold it a moment the way the brahmin held his bundle. If you pray, set it before an image or simply lift it and say a name you love, then eat or drink it as prasad; if you don't, give it in your mind to someone you love, and let the gladness of giving be enough.

987.title: Ganesha's song comes first
987.hook: the harmonium is ready, the room is full, and the first song goes to the god of beginnings
987.carry: honor Ganesha first: he clears the road
987.tomorrow: what does Om Namah Shivaya actually mean?
987.howItsDone: At a kirtan a leader often sings a line and the group sings it back, with harmonium, drum and hand cymbals; some groups open the evening with a song to Ganesha, who is honored before beginnings.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: This week the Bhagavata's tenth book went past the cowherd years: a teacher's fee, a letter, a jewel, and Sudama's handful of rice. Now the stories turn into songs.
screen: `THE BHAGAVATA'S TENTH BOOK.` · `PAST THE COWHERD YEARS.` · `NOW, THE SONGS.`

segments.voice: A rug on the floor, a harmonium in the middle of it, hand cymbals beside a drum. People drift in and sit cross-legged. Some know every word. Some have never been to a kirtan and are already worried about singing badly. The leader presses a key, the drone begins, and before any song to Krishna or Shiva, the first line goes out to someone else: an elephant-headed god, with a broken tusk and a sweet in one hand. The room sings it back. Why start there?
screen: `A RUG, A HARMONIUM, A DRUM.` → `THE DRONE BEGINS.` → `THE FIRST SONG GOES TO GANESHA.`

segments.voice: Kirtan is singing the names and glories of God together, often as call and response: the leader sings a line, the room sings it back. A repertoire is the songs a group knows by heart, the ones that can start without a songbook. For the next few days we'll build one, a song at a time, in roughly the order an evening might run. Some halls begin with Ganesha. Tradition honors him first before many beginnings: a wedding, a new house, a school year, a puja. He is called the remover of obstacles, and also their lord, the one who can place a block in the road or lift it. Tradition tells more than one story of why he goes first. In one, from the Shiva Purana, Shiva restores the boy to life with an elephant's head after a terrible quarrel, and declares that he will be worshipped before every other god. A Hindi aarti to him begins: Jai Ganesha, Jai Ganesha, Jai Ganesha Deva. Victory to Ganesha, victory to the god. The next line names his family: his mother is Parvati, his father is Mahadeva, the great god, Shiva. So the first song is partly a family introduction. And the evening doesn't begin with the hardest song. It begins by clearing the road. The nervous newcomer gets a simple line, sung slowly, and by the third round, it's in the room. In a kirtan, the first obstacle can be as small as opening your mouth.
screen: `KIRTAN: NAMES SUNG BACK AND FORTH.` · `A REPERTOIRE: SONGS KNOWN BY HEART.` · `GANESHA, HONORED FIRST.` · `HIS SONG CLEARS THE ROAD.` · then, large: `BEGIN BY CLEARING THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Let the shoulders drop and name one thing you're about to begin, a conversation, a piece of work, a trip, and then one thing that might block it: tiredness, worry, a person, a habit. Don't try to solve it; just see the obstacle clearly and set it down in front of you. If you pray, say Ganesha's name once, softly, as some Hindus do before a beginning; if not, simply rest with the road in front of you.
